claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy can be processed into a single-phase FCC microstructure by thermomechanical processing.
Systematic reduction or substitution of Mn changes the stacking-fault energy of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys.
Stacking-fault energy governs the activation of dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
The balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning controls alloy strength and ductility.
Mn modification changes the local chemical environment and electronic structure of the alloy.
Reducing or otherwise altering Mn lowers the stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation twinning.
Lower stacking-fault energy delays dislocation slip.
Enhanced twinning and delayed dislocation slip increase strain hardening.
Enhanced twinning and delayed dislocation slip increase both strength and ductility relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Reduced-Mn alloys should have lower stacking-fault energy than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Reduced-Mn alloys should exhibit more deformation twinning than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Reduced-Mn alloys should exhibit delayed dislocation motion relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Reduced-Mn alloys should exhibit greater strain hardening and failure strain than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase FCC and free of consequential phase separation, precipitation, and grain-boundary effects.
